problem: Inline marker *a moved from after 'estimation' to after 'others'; restore its source position.
replacement: It seems that people use two quite different standards when they publicly assess *a the actions of others. Sometimes they judge by the simple ideas of right and wrong found everywhere in the world; at other times they defer to a few very particular ideas that belong only to a certain age and country. These two standards often differ, and sometimes they conflict. Yet neither ever fully merges with the other or fully cancels it. At the height of its power, honor governs men’s will more than their belief. Even as they obey its commands without hesitation or complaint, they sense, by a faint but powerful instinct, a more general, more ancient and more sacred law, which they sometimes break but never stop acknowledging. Some actions have been considered virtuous and dishonorable at once; refusing to fight a duel is an example.

problem: 'the estimate which ought to be formed of them' became 'the value placed on them', dropping the normative sense.
replacement: I think these peculiarities can be explained otherwise than by the mere whims of particular individuals and nations, which until now has been the usual way of reasoning on the subject. Humanity has general and lasting needs, and these have given rise to moral laws. Everywhere and always, people have attached blame and shame to neglecting those laws: breaking them was “to do ill,” and “to do well” was to follow them. Within this vast association of the human race, smaller associations have formed, which are called nations; and within those nations, further divisions have taken the names of classes or castes. Each of these associations is, so to speak, a separate kind of human being. It differs in no essential way from the mass of humanity, yet to some extent it stands apart and has needs of its own. These special needs account for the changes, varying in degree from country to country, in how human actions are viewed and in the judgment that ought to be passed on them. It is the general and permanent interest of mankind that people should not kill one another; but it may happen to be the particular and temporary interest of a people or a class to justify homicide, or even to honor it.

problem: 'Nothing yields less to the mind than an abstract idea' is unnatural and unclear for 'unproductive'.
replacement: Honor is simply the particular rule, grounded in a particular state of society, by which a people or a class hands out praise or blame. Nothing is less fruitful to the mind than an abstract idea, so I hurry to bring in facts and examples to show what I mean.

problem: 'liberality' rendered 'lavishness', which tilts toward waste; he means open-handed giving.
replacement: In some cases feudal honor demanded revenge and branded forgiveness of insults as shameful; in others it sternly ordered men to master their own passions and to forget themselves. It did not make humanity or kindness its law, but it praised generosity; it valued open-handedness above benevolence; it allowed men to get rich by gambling or war, but not by work; it preferred great crimes to small earnings; it was less repelled by covetousness than by miserliness; it often sanctioned violence, but always condemned cunning and treachery as contemptible. These fantastic ideas did not come solely from the whims of those who held them. A class that has placed itself at the head of all others and above them, and that constantly strains to keep that high position, must honor above all the virtues that stand out for dignity and splendor and that combine easily with pride and love of power. Such men would not hesitate to turn the natural order of conscience upside down in order to put those virtues ahead of all others. One can even imagine that some of the bolder and more brilliant vices would readily be ranked above the quiet, unassuming virtues. The mere existence of such a class in society makes these things unavoidable.

problem: 'perhaps' to 'might even' sharpens the hedge ('even' added).
replacement: Any nation would give us similar grounds for observation. As I have already remarked, whenever men gather as a distinct community, the notion of honor immediately grows up among them, that is, a system of opinions of their own about what deserves blame or praise; and these special rules always originate in the community’s special habits and interests. To a certain extent this applies to democratic communities as well as to others, as we shall now prove by the example of the Americans. *c Some vague ideas of the old aristocratic honor of Europe can still be found scattered among Americans’ opinions. But these inherited opinions are few, they have little root in the country, and little power. They are like a religion that still has some temples standing, though men have stopped believing in it. Yet amid these half-erased notions of foreign honor, some new opinions have sprung up, which make up what may be called, in our day, American honor. I have shown how the Americans are constantly driven into commerce and industry. Their origin, their social condition, their political institutions, and even the place they live all push them irresistibly in this direction. Their present condition, then, is that of an almost exclusively manufacturing and commercial association, set in the midst of a new and boundless country, which their chief aim is to explore for profit. This is the trait that most distinguishes the American people from all others at present. All the quiet virtues that give the community a regular movement and encourage business will therefore be held in particular honor by that people, and neglecting them will bring public contempt. All the more turbulent virtues, which often dazzle but more often disturb society, will on the contrary rank lower in this same people’s estimation. They may be neglected without losing the community’s esteem; acquiring them would perhaps risk losing it.
